turns.question: Tell me about a time you fixed a bug that affected users.
turns.answer: In my internship our checkout sometimes charged customers twice. I was asked to find out why. I read the payment logs and saw that the client retried a request after a timeout while the first one had already succeeded. I added an idempotency key to the payment request and a unique index on it in the database, and I wrote a test that sends the same request twice. After the release we had zero double charges in the next month, and support stopped getting those tickets. I learned to check retries first whenever something happens twice.

turns.question: Describe a time you received critical feedback on your code.
turns.answer: On my first big pull request my reviewer said the function was 200 lines long and hard to test. I asked her to show me one part she found confusing, then I split the function into four smaller ones with clear names and added unit tests for each. The second review took ten minutes instead of a day. Since then I keep my pull requests under 300 lines and I ask for an early look when I am unsure about the design.

notes: Both stories have a clear order, own actions, numbers and a lesson: high scores at junior level.

turns.question: Tell me about a time you had to deliver under a tight deadline.
turns.answer: Two days before a launch, our load test showed the API timing out at 500 requests per second. I owned the search endpoint, so I profiled it and found an N+1 query that loaded each product's category separately. I rewrote it as one join, added an index on the category id, and reran the test: we handled 2,000 requests per second with p95 under 200 milliseconds and launched on time. Afterwards I added the load test to our CI so it runs before every release.

turns.question: How would you make a slow API endpoint faster?
turns.answer: First I would measure where the time goes, with logging or a profiler. If the database query is slow I would add an index on the column we filter by, and if the same data is read often I would cache it, for example in Redis with an expiry time, so most requests don't hit the database.

turns.question: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
turns.answer: A process has its own memory and a thread runs inside a process and shares its memory with the other threads. Threads are lighter to start, but because they share memory you need locks to avoid two threads changing the same data at once.

notes: Correct, clear basics: good for a junior. Compare with same-answer-senior.

turns.question: Tell me about a time you improved a process on your team.
turns.answer: Our releases were painful, so I wrote a script that automated most of the release steps and the team started using it for every release after that.

turns.question: What changed after the team started using it?
turns.answer: Releases went from about three hours of manual steps to twenty minutes, and we stopped forgetting the database migration, which had broken production twice that quarter. I also wrote a short page in our wiki so new people could run it.
